title: Review of Submarine Cable Landing License Rules and Procedures To Assess Evolving National Security, Law Enforcement, Foreign Policy, and Trade Policy Risks
summary:
The Federal Communications Commission just modernized how the U.S. licenses and oversees undersea internet cables. The new rules aim to speed up deployment while tightening security, especially against companies tied to governments the Commerce Department labels as foreign adversaries, such as China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, Cuba, and the Maduro regime in Venezuela.

What changes most: applications from companies owned, controlled, or directed by those governments will face a strong presumption of denial, and proposals to land a cable in those countries will likely be rejected. Licensees are now barred from new or extended capacity deals that would let an adversary‑linked entity install, own, or manage the terminal equipment at a U.S. landing site. New cable projects must certify they will not use equipment or services on the government’s list of known security risks, and existing licensees must pledge not to add such gear going forward. All applicants and licensees must create and maintain a cybersecurity and physical security risk plan, signed by a senior executive. The FCC also clarified that a license is needed if any part of a domestic cable runs beyond U.S. territorial waters, and it formally defines a “submarine cable system” to include the landing‑site terminal equipment.

Oversight will be more targeted and, in some places, simpler. The FCC kept the 25‑year license term, set a three‑year deadline to put a licensed cable into service, and streamlined several filing and modification steps. It eliminated a duplicative capacity report and will collect clearer, more useful data in a single annual filing, now also covering domestic cables. Certain licensees tied to adversary countries will file an annual report with ownership, operations, and security details. The agency will share confidential capacity data with national security partners to speed risk review, while keeping precise locations of sensitive facilities non‑public.

Who benefits: U.S. national security, public safety, and the broader digital economy that relies on resilient, trusted global connectivity. Legitimate investors and operators should also see quicker, clearer processes. Who may be negatively affected: companies linked to adversary governments, firms relying on equipment the government deems risky, and some operators facing new compliance work and costs. The FCC estimates added industry‑wide costs at about $2.5 million per year, and it stopped short of ordering any “rip and replace” of existing gear.

Many provisions take effect November 26, 2025, with some reporting pieces delayed until federal approvals are finalized.
